connect.idea: Graphics lives in a world of gaps. You have a few measurements—a handful of keyframes, some sparse pose estimates from cameras, a texture draped across a mesh, a handful of seed points—but you need a complete picture everywhere. The connective tissue is what fills those gaps: smooth blending between nearby known values, finding the closest matching pattern when you face something new, reshaping coordinates so relationships stay intact as you move from one frame or space to another, and tracking how pieces fit together (topology). This is not the flashy machinery of lighting and color; it is the quiet bookkeeping that lets every fancy technique work. The core realization is that the world does not jump: between two neighboring measurements, the truth stays close to their blend, and relationships—which pose is nearest, how a cloth drapes, which pixels influence which output pixels—survive honest rearrangement of space.
connect.why: It works because smooth functions have no sudden cliffs. If you measure a surface at two nearby points and blend the values linearly (or with any smooth curve), you are extremely close to the real answer almost everywhere between them. Topological relationships—connectivity, ordering, which-is-nearest—do not depend on coordinates; a translation, rotation, or nonlinear warping changes where things sit but not how they relate. You can solve a hard problem in a convenient space (aligned pose space, latent coordinate space, flattened texture space) where relationships are simple, then carry the solution back to the original frame without breaking it. The catch is that this only holds for truly smooth underlying phenomena; if your data has cracks, isolated islands, or genuinely discontinuous transitions, blending and coordinate tricks hit a wall.
connect.math: The mathematical principle is continuity plus structure-preserving change. Continuity means that nearby inputs should usually have nearby outputs: two nearby points on a surface should have similar color, similar position, or similar motion unless there is a real edge or tear between them. That one belief lets you fill missing values by blending known neighbors instead of inventing each unknown value from scratch. Structure-preserving change means that when you move from one coordinate system to another, the relationships that matter should survive the move: which points are adjacent, which direction is forward, which samples are close, and which pieces remain connected. This is why graphics uses interpolation, nearest-neighbor search, coordinate transforms, maps between surfaces, and graph connections so often. They are all ways of saying: keep the relationships stable while you carry information from where you know it to where you need it. The important object is not a single number but a relationship: between two frames, two meshes, two views, or two samples. The danger is also clear from first principles. If the thing being filled in is not smooth, or if the mapping tears, folds, or changes neighborhood order, then blending makes false middle values and nearest-neighbor logic points to the wrong source. Good graphics methods spend much of their effort detecting those breaks, choosing better neighborhoods, or building a space where the relationship is smoother than it was in raw pixels or raw coordinates.
connect.family: This family is made of papers that face the same practical problem: they know something only at scattered places and must make it usable everywhere. Some papers fill missing image values, animation frames, surface samples, or texture coordinates. Others move information across spaces: from one camera view to another, from one body to a different body, from a high-dimensional motion library to a compact search space, or from a rough surface representation to a clean one. Their shared failure mode is naive copying. Copy a pixel without respecting its neighbors and you get seams. Copy a pose without respecting body proportions and the motion breaks. Search raw data without a good distance structure and similar things do not actually end up near each other. The common mathematical move is to build a trustworthy relation first, then use it to transfer information. That relation might be a smooth interpolation rule, a nearest-neighbor index, a mesh map, a learned coordinate space, or a graph of who connects to whom. The papers are siblings because they all treat graphics as a problem of carrying known information across gaps without breaking the underlying arrangement.
connect.dots: The papers show this single move running through almost every problem. Blending pixels: Lucky High Dynamic Range learns to mix bracketed photos by training once and then applying the learned blend to new photos. Interpolation: LayerInbetween smoothly fills missing animation frames by tracking stroke strokes across layers and warping progressively. Manifold k-NN finds nearest neighbors by building a recursive hierarchy of spatial regions so you skip checking far-away points. Retargeting motion to a new character works by learning to adaptively adjust anchor points, then smoothly warping spatial relationships to fit the new body (Spatially Adaptive Interaction Guidance). Coordinate changes: PAColorHolo transforms distorted laser colors back to true colors via learned neural coordinate mappings. NeuBase preserves four sacred properties—linearity, locality, smoothness, and affine invariance—so neural deformations stay safe under coordinate changes. TwinPose reconstructs 3D pose from multiple 2D camera views by fitting poses into a learned person-specific subspace so each body stays within its natural movement patterns. MotionBricks compresses 350k motion clips into a learned latent space where similar poses cluster, then interpolates between motion primitives at runtime. The connecting thread: every approach assumes smoothness or learned distance structure, then uses blending, nearest-matching, or coordinate warping to carry information from known places to unknown ones.
connect.picture: Imagine you have a few paint color swatches and need to fill a whole wall. You do not jump from swatch to swatch; you blend neighboring swatches to paint the in-between smoothly. Or imagine tracing a person's hand in a video where you see frames 1 and 5 clearly but frames 2, 3, 4 are blurry. You do not guess randomly; you smoothly warp where the hand was in frame 1 toward where it is in frame 5, interpolating the in-between positions. Or imagine moving a dance routine from one dancer's body to another's; you do not copy joint positions exactly (because bodies are different shapes), but you remember spatial relationships—which joints are near each other, which move together—and gently reshape those relationships to fit the new body. All of these are the same move: use what you know, blend smoothly to fill gaps, preserve the relationships that matter.

curve.idea: Start with a simple physical fact: bend a piece of paper and it stays paper—the rubber doesn't change, the thickness doesn't multiply. Yet the shape has clearly changed. Curvature is the answer to a practical question: how much is this surface bent, right here, in this direction? It's not about where the surface sits in space; it's about how tightly the surface wraps back on itself. The moment you want to simulate a bending shell, predict where light touches an edge, understand what makes one material stiff and another flexible, or figure out if a point sits inside a complicated shape, you need to measure curvature. Curvature is an intrinsic property of a surface—the amount of twist and bending embedded in the surface itself, independent of where you put it or how you rotate it. Once you can measure curvature at every point, you can describe how any surface behaves: smooth surfaces have low curvature, creased origami has sharp curvature changes, and a sphere has constant curvature everywhere.
curve.why: Curvature works as a reliable, stable measurement because it reflects how the surface itself is built, not an artifact of your coordinate system. If you measure the angle between neighboring patches on a mesh or track how the surface normal rotates as you move along it, you get the same curvature answer whether you rotated the whole object or not. This stability means curvature becomes a quantifiable constraint: you can preserve it during deformation, use it to rank which features matter most (peaks and valleys), and build energy functions that reward shapes with desired curvature properties. When things break, it's usually at singularities—points where the surface has a crack or a pinch—or where discrete approximations fail to capture infinitesimal changes. But for smooth regions, curvature is as trustworthy as geometry gets.
curve.math: The mathematical principle is local shape measurement. A surface may look like one continuous object, but a computer only sees samples: triangles, points, patches, signed distances, or tiny neighborhoods. Curvature asks what happens when you zoom in at one spot and compare nearby directions. If the surface normal barely changes as you move, the region is flat. If the normal turns quickly, the surface is bending sharply. If it bends one way in one direction and the opposite way in another, you have a saddle. That simple idea becomes the basis for measuring smoothness, sharpness, thickness, folds, creases, and stability. The important point is that curvature is not just decoration; it tells you how a shape resists bending, how light changes across it, where silhouettes and boundaries form, and which features are real rather than sampling noise. In continuous mathematics this is measured through derivatives: not just where the surface is, but how its direction changes as you move. In discrete graphics it is estimated from neighboring triangles, points, or implicit fields. The risk is that samples can lie. A coarse mesh can hide a sharp bend, noise can pretend to be curvature, and a crack can make the local measurement meaningless. Good methods therefore treat curvature as a local truth that must be estimated carefully and preserved only where the surface is actually smooth enough for the measurement to mean something.
curve.family: The curvature family contains papers that need to know what a shape is doing locally before they can act globally. Some papers simulate thin shells, folds, bending materials, or contact, where local bending determines force. Some reconstruct surfaces from points or implicit fields, where local shape tells the algorithm how to fill missing geometry without flattening important features. Some render or integrate along boundaries, where the changing direction of a surface controls how light, visibility, or winding behaves. Their common failure mode is treating a shape as just a pile of positions. Positions alone tell you where samples are, but not how the surface bends between them or how it should behave under motion, smoothing, cutting, or illumination. The common mathematical move is to measure local change in direction and use that measurement as a constraint, signal, or energy. The papers are siblings because they all depend on the same first-principles fact: a surface has meaning in how it bends from one tiny patch to the next, not only in where its points happen to sit.
curve.dots: Across these seventeen papers, curvature plays the same hidden role under wildly different disguises. In thin shells (Better Bending), curvature captures bending by measuring angle changes between neighboring triangles; in origami (Lamination Framework), the same idea becomes fold angles redirecting strain. For inside-outside tests (Winding Numbers), curvature allows fast approximations by using Taylor expansions—the curve's local bending tells you its behavior from a distance. In materials science (Mechanical Cloaking, Wood Decay), curvature of grain or internal structure determines how forces propagate. For rendering, Robust Boundary Integrals uses kernel smoothing to handle light bouncing at sharp edges—curvature of the boundary itself. Even in topology (Persistence-guided Simplification), curvature-like measures rank which bumps and holes are real features worth keeping. Implicit surfaces (PhaseTree, Gaussian Process Surfaces, Points as Tori), signed distances, and ray tracing all lean on curvature to understand geometry locally. The thread is unmistakable: measure the shape's bending, and you unlock the ability to simulate, render, optimize, and classify everything that follows.
curve.picture: Imagine running your fingertip along the rim of a bowl versus the edge of a flat plate. On the bowl, your finger curves inward sharply—that's high curvature. On the plate, it barely bends—low curvature. Curvature is exactly that: the amount your surface is bent at any point. Once you know how bent a surface is everywhere, you can predict how it stretches when you squeeze it (like pressing the bowl), where water will pool (topology follows curvature), and even how easily light will scatter off it (light curves when surfaces are curved). That's why every picture-making and shape-making problem in graphics circles back to one question: how bent is this surface?

integrate.idea: In graphics, nearly every quantity that matters — a pixel's color, a surface's charge, a fluid's flow — comes from an infinity of tiny contributions arriving from all directions and times at once. Light is the prime example: a single point on your screen receives photons from countless paths through the scene, scattered by materials, bouncing off surfaces, arriving over a continuous spectrum of directions. The pixel's final color is literally the sum of all those contributions. But you cannot enumerate an infinite sum. The core insight is that you never need to: most of the contribution is concentrated in a few large peaks. By breaking the infinite total into finite chunks — sampling along rays, discretizing time, chopping space into voxels — you can add up the chunks and trust that as you make the chunks smaller, your finite sum closes in on the true infinite answer. This is integration: turning an uncountable infinity into a countable approximation.
integrate.why: Integration works because continuous quantities are not random and scattered; they have structure. Most of the contribution comes from regions of high density — where light is bright, where mass clusters, where forces concentrate — and these regions are finite in number and size. The guarantees come from the mathematics: any continuous total can be trapped between an over-estimate and an under-estimate (by summing tall and short rectangles under a curve), and as you chop your intervals thinner, both traps squeeze tighter and tighter toward the true answer. This squeezing never stops — you can always get closer — but you reach the 'close enough' point long before infinity. The method fails only when the quantity has wild, unbounded spikes (infinite variance), but in graphics, real physics forces smoothness: light refracts gradually, materials blend, heat diffuses. The structure of physics itself guarantees that your approximation converges.
integrate.math: The mathematical principle is turning a continuous total into a controlled finite sum. A pixel color is not one event; it is the total effect of light from many directions, distances, wavelengths, and bounces. A volume density, pressure field, heat value, or material response is similar: the quantity at one place depends on many tiny contributions spread through space or time. Integration is the rule for adding those contributions when there are too many to list. From first principles, imagine slicing a smooth quantity into small pieces. Each piece is small enough that its value is almost constant inside the slice, so the piece contributes roughly value times size. Add all pieces and you approximate the total. Make the pieces smaller and the approximation gets closer because each slice lies less about what happens inside it. In graphics the pieces might be ray samples, surface patches, voxels, photons, random paths, time bins, or boundary segments. The crucial mathematical object is the accumulated measure: the total amount of light, mass, probability, flow, or influence over a continuous region. The danger is that some regions contribute far more than others. If the method samples the wrong places, a tiny bright caustic, sharp boundary, or high-density volume can dominate the true answer while being missed by the approximation. Strong methods either choose pieces adaptively, sample with probability, or transform the integral into a form where the important contributions are easier to capture.
integrate.family: This family is made of papers that face a total-too-large-to-add-directly problem. Rendering papers add light along rays or over paths. Volume and material papers add absorption, scattering, density, or response through space. Imaging and inverse problems add many hidden contributions and then try to recover the source that produced the observed total. Geometry papers turn inside-outside tests, boundary effects, or field reconstruction into sums over surfaces or volumes. Their shared failure mode is pretending that one sample or one local value is enough. One light ray is not a pixel. One point on a boundary is not a shape. One photon arrival is not a measurement. The common mathematical move is to define the correct total first, then approximate it with enough structure that the approximation is honest. These papers are siblings because they all make the same trade: accept that the real quantity is continuous and enormous, then design a finite summation that preserves the important parts of that continuous truth.
integrate.dots: Across these 16 papers, integration appears in disguises that all share one move: formulate the answer as a continuous sum, then approximate it with samples or pieces. In volumetric rendering (GenPIE, Sample Matching, Efficient Fur), light traveling through smoke or fog is a ray integral — light lost to scattering plus light arriving from all directions — broken into small segments along the ray, evaluated stochastically. In holography (HoloPathTracer), the wavefront is an integral over all light paths; Monte Carlo path tracing randomly samples paths and weights them to approximate this path integral. In inverse problems (Thermal Non-Line-of-Sight, Gradient Domain Reconstruction), the forward model is an integral (convolution of light transport with a kernel, or a Poisson integral); the solver inverts this by treating it as an optimization over gradients or learned features, then reconstructs. In numerical PDEs (Schrödinger Bridges, Biharmonic Diffusion), the solution satisfies a differential equation (which locally sums up small changes); the solver samples random walks or boundary conditions to estimate the integral form. In imaging (Hi-SPAD, Hyperspectral), photon arrivals are random samples; their histogram is the integral of the spectrum. In geometry (Antipodal Winding Numbers), point-in-shape tests use boundary integrals expressed as ray-surface intersections; the method transforms the volume integral into a surface integral, which is far cheaper to compute. In differentiable rendering (Closed-Form Convolution, Differentiable Neutron Transport), you need the derivative of an integral; by sampling the integrand or using convolution, you can backpropagation through the sum. The single thread: pick the right decomposition of your integral, evaluate it piecewise, and sum.
integrate.picture: Imagine sunlight hitting a table. The table's color is not determined by just the one ray of sunlight coming straight down from the sun — it is the sum of light arriving from every angle: bounced off clouds, reflected from nearby walls, scattered by the air itself, each contributing a tiny bit to the final brightness you see. You cannot measure each of those infinite directions separately, so instead you point a light meter in a few key directions, measure in each, and add them up. The more directions you measure, the closer your sum gets to the true total. By noon tomorrow, when you have sampled more directions and time has smoothed out the variations, your sum will be almost exact. This is exactly what a rendering algorithm does: sample the light from many directions and times along a ray, add them up, and trust that enough samples will converge to the true color.

modes.idea: Real objects and images are not formless blobs. Every shape has favorite ways it wants to sit, bounce, and move. Every image has large simple structures layered underneath the fine chaotic details. A mode is one of these favorite patterns — the coarse shadow under complex light, the dominant vibration of a drum, the underlying frequency that shows up across frames of video. The insight: instead of storing or computing with all the raw data (every pixel, every triangle, every tiny vibration), you can describe almost anything by listing just its handful of dominant modes — the most important ways it naturally wants to be. This changes a massive, messy problem into a small, clean one.
modes.why: Modes work because the real world is fundamentally smooth and biased. Things do not wiggle at random scales — they concentrate their energy in a few large, organized patterns and scatter only crumbs in the fine chaotic details. A tuning fork vibrates in one pure pitch far louder than in any other. A landscape has a few major hills and ridges under the scattered grass. A face in video has gross motion (the head turning) that drowns out the fine motion (skin pores shifting). When you keep only the dominant modes and discard the rest, you throw away almost nothing that matters, but you shrink your data and silence the noise. The mode approach works because it trusts that nature has already done the hard work of organization — your job is just to find and keep what nature emphasized.
modes.math: The mathematical principle is basis representation: describe a complicated signal as a mixture of simpler natural patterns. A raw image, motion, deformation, sound, or field can have thousands or millions of values. But those values often move together. A face turning left changes many pixels in a coordinated way. A vibrating object bends through a few dominant shapes. A texture has broad bands of detail plus smaller ripples. A basis is a set of reusable patterns; a mode is one pattern in that set. Instead of storing every raw value, you store how much of each pattern is present. This matters because many systems concentrate most of their energy or visual meaning in only a few modes. Keep the large modes and you keep the identity of the object; discard tiny modes and you mostly remove noise or detail the viewer does not need. Mathematically, this is a change of coordinates from raw samples to pattern weights. The important act is separation: coarse from fine, loud from quiet, stable from noisy, shared motion from accidental variation. The risk is that the chosen basis may not match the object. If the natural patterns are wrong, important detail gets thrown away or unrelated effects get mixed together. Good methods therefore learn, derive, or adapt the modes so the compact representation follows the actual shape, material, image, or motion rather than imposing a convenient but false pattern.
modes.family: This family contains papers that reduce a huge graphics object to a smaller set of meaningful coordinates. Some work in frequency bands, keeping broad image or lighting patterns separate from fine texture. Some work in motion or deformation modes, representing a body or elastic object by the few ways it naturally moves. Some build latent spaces where similar shapes, poses, or appearances cluster around shared patterns. Their common failure mode is raw representation. Raw pixels, raw vertices, and raw time samples are expensive and easily confused because every small value is treated as equally important. The common mathematical move is to find the patterns that carry most of the signal and do the work there. These papers are siblings because they all assume that graphics data is not arbitrary noise. It has preferred rhythms, shapes, bands, and directions. Once those are found, the problem becomes smaller, cleaner, faster, and often more stable.
modes.dots: This single idea wears radically different disguises across the 14 papers in this group. In video compression, modes become the frequencies in a Fourier decomposition — the paper works in the frequency domain where motion prediction becomes trivial, because each frequency channel evolves independently over time. In character animation, modes are the natural degrees of freedom of a skeleton — ACT treats the full coupled pose space as a harmonic system, where motion flows along the smoothest paths the body naturally prefers. In volumetric rendering with Gabor fields, modes are the oriented sine waves that define detail at each scale — you disable high-frequency modes to speed up rendering. In material appearance (relighting papers), modes are the basis functions of lighting — a face's response to light from any angle is built by mixing a few learned patterns, each one a mode of how light-skin interaction works. In physics simulation (eigenvalue problems, Koopman deformables), modes become the literal vibration patterns of a structure — elastic objects deform via their natural resonance modes, and time integration becomes multiplication by the corresponding mode amplitude rather than numerical stepping. In holography, modes are frequency bands in the interference pattern — splitting the design across different frequency modes lets you avoid crosstalk. In procedural texturing, modes are the wave frequencies that define local detail. In mesh-based signal learning (Matérn noise), modes are the frequency components that remain stable under mesh deformation. The throughline: everywhere you look, the problem of storing, compressing, or simulating something complex reduces to finding the thing's natural modes and working in that basis instead.
modes.picture: Imagine plucking a guitar string. One pluck excites many possible vibrations, but only a few matter: the fundamental (deep note), the first overtone (higher), the second (even higher). These are the string's modes — its natural rhythms. You could describe the string's motion by tracking billions of tiny points, but really it is just the fundamental vibrating loudly plus faint whispers of overtones. Ignore those whispers and the string still sounds unmistakably like itself. This is what modes do for images, shapes, and motion: you keep the fundamental and the clear overtones, throw away the noise, and the thing still looks and feels like itself — but now it fits in a postcard instead of a filing cabinet.

optimize.idea: Nearly every problem in making pictures and shapes on a computer comes down to this: you have some arrangement (cloth draped on a body, a 3D model's vertex positions, a laser's path through glass, layers of fiber in a composite beam) and infinitely many ways to place or adjust it. Most arrangements are obviously wrong—the cloth tears, the shape tears, light scatters, the beam snaps. A thoughtful person asks: what single measure could tell me how wrong an arrangement is? Maybe total stretching energy, or distance from a reference shape, or rays landing where they shouldn't. Once you have that measure—call it a score—the insight is mechanical: just keep moving in the direction that lowers the score, the way a marble rolls downhill. Stop when no small step down exists. That stopping point is your answer. This is optimization: invent a score, then find the arrangement that makes it smallest while respecting any hard rules (the cloth stays connected, the shape stays manifold, the beam holds a target load). The move appears everywhere because it solves the deepest problem in graphics—turning high-level intent ("cloth should drape naturally", "shape should be sturdy") into concrete geometry.
optimize.why: The reason this works is rooted in the shape of a score itself. If you imagine plotting a score against all possible arrangements, it forms a landscape—mostly bumpy, but always with one critical property: the downhill direction at any point tells you exactly which small step reduces the score. This is geometry, not magic. Even if the landscape is wrinkled (many local dips), stepping downhill reliably fills a decent dip because you cannot step uphill by accident. You halt where you've reached a resting point—a place where no neighboring arrangement scores better. In many cases (when the landscape is convex, shaped like a bowl), that resting point is the unique global best. In rougher landscapes you find a good enough answer determined by where you started. The method also gracefully handles hard constraints: you can reformulate them as steep penalties in the score, or solve them as part of the step-finding logic itself. Physics validates the intuition—real materials under stress settle into their lowest-energy state, so optimizing energy exactly mimics how the world behaves.
optimize.math: The mathematical principle is choosing an arrangement by defining what wrongness means. A graphics task usually has many possible answers: many cloth shapes, many camera poses, many material layouts, many neural weights, many meshes. Optimization begins by turning preference into a number. This number is low when the answer is good and high when it violates the goal. It might measure stretch, distance from data, mismatch in an image, physical energy, instability, computation cost, or unfair deviation from a constraint. Once wrongness is a number, nearby arrangements can be compared. The slope of that number tells which tiny changes make the answer worse; moving the opposite way makes it better. If there are hard rules, such as no self-intersection or fixed boundary points, the method either builds them into the search or punishes violations so strongly that invalid answers are avoided. The key mathematical object is the landscape of possible answers. A simple bowl-shaped landscape has one best point. A rough landscape has many resting points, so the starting point and search path matter. This is why optimization is powerful but not magic. It converts intent into a solvable problem, but the quality of the answer depends on whether the wrongness number actually captures what the artist, camera, object, or physics demands.
optimize.family: The optimization family is made of papers that share a single shape of problem: there is no direct formula for the answer, but there is a way to score candidate answers. Cloth capture scores how well a simulated cloth matches observations while obeying fabric behavior. Shape design scores fit, stress, smoothness, or manufacturability. Inverse rendering scores how well guessed scene properties reproduce an image. Neural and procedural methods score prediction error or cost. Their shared failure mode is hand-tuning or greedy local fixing. Adjusting one vertex, ray, parameter, or panel at a time can improve the visible symptom while breaking the rest of the system. The common mathematical move is to make all the demands visible inside one score and then search for a low-scoring arrangement. These papers are siblings because they all translate a graphics wish into an energy, loss, or objective: not a slogan, but a number that can be minimized.
optimize.dots: Look across the SIGGRAPH papers and the single idea wears a dozen disguises. In YASPS, contact and deformation both minimize total energy; the algorithm computes the precise slopes and curvatures of that landscape to land exactly at equilibrium without trial-and-error. In cloth capture (High-Fidelity 4D Cloth), the 3D model deforms to a shape where elastic strain plus contact penalties are minimized—the score measures wrongness, and solving it reconstructs the real cloth. In fabric capture (Fiber-level Woven Fabric), a microscope image is matched by optimizing fiber parameters: position, angle, thickness. The score is pixel-level image error, and each step of optimization refines fibers until the rendered output matches the photo. In shape optimization (Stress-Aware Panelization, Co-Optimization of Composite Layers), the score measures both geometric fit and structural performance—stress and stiffness weigh against deviation from a design intent. Materials layout (AtomSlicer) enforces direction fields and constant extrusion width simultaneously by breaking the problem into layered constraints and solving them as a coupled minimization. In mesh untangling (Untangling Surfaces), the score combines global entanglement energy and local self-intersection penalties; minimizing them unravels knots in complex 3D models. Motion retargeting (ReActor) optimizes a robot's trajectory such that the physics simulator says it's physically feasible—the score is trajectory parameters, and the constraint is "physics says this is safe." Even in neural methods (SAND), the optimization assigns network depth adaptively: the score is computation per region, and the method solves which region gets which size. The unifying move: measure wrongness, step downhill, stop at rest. Every paper is that idea applied to a different kind of wrongness and a different domain.
optimize.picture: Imagine threading a bead along a wrinkled wire hanging between two posts. The bead has weight, so it wants to slide downhill. You don't need to think about which direction to pull—just let it roll. It will settle into a dip where no push left or right makes it slide lower. If the wire is smooth (convex), that dip is the lowest point on the entire wire. If the wire is bumpy, the bead lands in one of many dips, but it's always a dip—a resting place. That bead-on-wire is exactly optimization: the wire's shape is your score landscape, the bead's position is an arrangement (vertex locations, fiber angles, material layout), and rolling downhill is the algorithm. Stop when the bead stops moving. That's your answer.

random.idea: Graphics must solve problems with infinite possibilities: every direction a ray of light could bounce, every way to arrange furniture in a room, every path to carry a probability distribution forward. You cannot check all of them—the space is too large. Instead, you choose a limited set of possibilities at random, compute what happens for each, and average the results. The critical insight is that if you choose these random samples independently and fairly, the average of your results will, on average, equal the true answer you seek—as if the randomness had simply cancelled itself out and revealed the underlying truth. Your finite sample size introduces error, but that error shrinks predictably as you add more samples. By aiming your random selections at the places where the answer varies most dramatically, you can make the error shrink much faster, turning a speckled guess into a sharp answer.
random.why: The guarantee comes from a simple but powerful fact: when many independent random samples are drawn fairly from a space, their average converges to the true total or integral you are chasing. This is not magic—it is a consequence of how probability actually works. Each random sample pulls you toward the right answer with equal probability; the pulls that miss high and low cancel each other out statistically, leaving the honest value. The error left behind is dominated by variance—how scattered your samples are around that true answer—and this variance shrinks at a known, predictable rate (roughly as one divided by the square root of the number of samples). This is where strategy enters: if you arrange your samples to crowd into regions where the answer changes rapidly—where a small shift in input produces a big shift in output—you reduce the variance in those regions, which dampens the overall error faster. Conversely, placing samples uniformly in regions where the answer is flat wastes computational budget, since one sample there contains nearly the same information as any other.
random.math: The mathematical principle is unbiased estimation with controlled error. When the true answer is a large total over many possibilities, a random sample is useful only if it is chosen by a rule that gives every contribution its proper chance to be represented. If that condition holds, each sample may be noisy, but the average of many samples points to the right total. The noise does not vanish because each sample is correct; it vanishes because independent errors tend to cancel. The remaining uncertainty is variance: how widely individual samples bounce around the true value. A method improves when it lowers variance for the same amount of work. That is why graphics uses importance sampling, adaptive sampling, random walks, diffusion noise, and stochastic particles. They are all ways to spend samples where the answer is most uncertain, most energetic, or most visually important. The key mathematical object is not randomness by itself but the expected value: the long-run average the samples would approach if you could repeat the process forever. The risk is bias. If the sampling rule quietly misses some kind of path, particle, direction, or event, the average becomes confidently wrong. Good methods therefore track both fairness and variance: sample smartly, but weight samples so the final average still represents the true underlying total.
random.family: This family contains papers that use randomness because the complete set of possibilities is too large to enumerate. Rendering papers sample light paths instead of tracing every possible bounce. Physics papers use random walks or particles to estimate solutions that would otherwise require dense grids. Generative papers start from noise and gradually remove it because the final object is easier to form as a sequence of uncertain refinements. Inverse problems use random evidence to probe hidden structure. Their shared failure mode is exhaustive computation. Trying every path, every particle interaction, every layout, or every hidden cause is impossible. The common mathematical move is to replace complete enumeration with a fair random experiment whose average means something. These papers are siblings because they do not use randomness as decoration. They use it as a disciplined measuring tool: a way to touch an enormous space through a small number of carefully weighted glimpses.
random.dots: Across the 24 papers here, this single principle wears many disguises. In path tracing (ray bouncing to render light), papers like 'Forget Superresolution, Sample Adaptively' and 'NILE' tackle the core problem: you have infinitely many directions a ray could scatter, and you cannot afford to trace them all. These papers use smart sampling—concentrating rays where the image is most complex or where light energy is concentrated—so fewer rays produce a sharper final picture. For solving physics equations on complex shapes (Poisson problems for heat, deformation, or fluids), 'Walk on Decomposed Subdomains' and 'Probe-based Walk on Spheres' employ random walks: they shuffle through space randomly, stepping from place to place, and the average outcome estimates what the true solution should be. In simulation, 'Spatiotemporal FLIP' and 'Stochastic geomorphological transport' inject randomness—jittering particles in time or space, or randomly perturbing sediment flow—to capture the natural chaos that deterministic simulation misses; the ensemble result averages into the physically correct pattern. In generative models ('CasLayout' diffusion, 'Grow3D' octrees), randomness is gradually removed in carefully orchestrated steps, where each step solves a simpler, noisier version of the final problem; the averaging across all those noisy intermediate states converges to realistic outputs. Even in inverse problems like 'Radiance Caching for Differentiable Path Tracing' and 'Inverse Rendering for Discrete X-Ray', the same principle holds: you cannot measure or compute the answer directly, so you gather noisy random evidence from the forward model and average it—using geometry-aware blending to crowd samples where the answer is uncertain. In all these cases, the same thread runs underneath: faced with infinity, you sample smart and average honestly.
random.picture: Imagine you are asked to estimate the total amount of water flowing down a mountain range, but you can only measure water flow at a handful of random points—you cannot measure everywhere. If you pick your measurement points carelessly (say, all in a flat valley), your average will be wildly wrong. But if you deliberately concentrate measurements at the steep cliffs and ridge lines where water rushes fastest, even a small number of measurements will average to almost the true total, because those high-energy regions dominate the answer. The mountain does not know you are only sampling a few points; the random measurements simply happen to land where they matter most, so the randomness dissolves and the hidden truth emerges.

solve.idea: In graphics, almost everything is a web of mutual dependencies. A hanging cloth doesn't decide its shape point by point — each bit pulls on its neighbors, which pull back. A 3D shape at rest balances internal forces. A material's properties emerge from how its tiny lattice structure fights back against stress. A surface being modeled must satisfy curve intersections, geometric constraints, and smoothness all at the same time. You cannot solve these things one piece at a time; if you settle one corner of the cloth, it changes everything else. The only way forward is to write down what "balanced" means — a massive set of equations where every constraint mentions every neighbor — and solve all of them together as a single unified problem. That solution exists and is unique (there is truly one state where everything is satisfied), but finding it requires treating the whole system at once, not as isolated local choices.
solve.why: The guarantee comes from physics itself. A real physical system at rest has reached a minimum-energy state: every force has stopped pushing, every stress has spread out evenly. That state is unique — you cannot have two different ways to balance the same cloth or the same shape simultaneously. When you write equations saying "force here equals zero" and "force there equals zero" at every point, you are encoding this physical truth into algebra. The system of equations has exactly one solution (or a discrete set if there are multiple distinct balanced arrangements), and that solution IS the physical reality. This is why solving the equations (even approximately on a computer) gets you the right answer: you are not guessing or iterating randomly, you are following mathematics that mirrors how the real world works. The method fails only when the system is over-constrained (you ask for something physically impossible) or under-constrained (you haven't specified enough to pin down a single answer).
solve.math: The mathematical principle is simultaneous constraint satisfaction. Many graphics systems are coupled: one point of cloth pulls another, one cell of a fluid pushes the next, one surface patch must meet another, one material cell changes the stress in its neighbors. A local choice is therefore not independent. Solving means writing all the local demands as equations and finding values that satisfy them together. The equations may say forces cancel, distances match, intersections occur at zero error, boundary values hold, or a field has the right smoothness. The important object is the unknown vector: all positions, velocities, pressures, weights, or field values collected into one joint answer. The solver changes that whole answer until every equation is close enough to true. This matters because coupled systems punish greedy thinking. Fix one corner of a cloth without updating the rest and the whole state becomes inconsistent. The guarantee depends on the equation structure. Some systems have one stable solution; some have several; some are ill-conditioned, meaning tiny input errors cause large output changes. Strong papers pay attention to conditioning, robustness, approximation, and hierarchy so the enormous solve is not just correct in theory but stable on real meshes, curves, and machines.
solve.family: The solve family contains papers where the answer is a balanced state, not a prediction made piece by piece. Physics papers solve for positions, forces, pressures, or material responses that must all agree. Geometry papers solve intersections, distances, winding relationships, or surface constraints that must be globally consistent. Holography and inverse design papers solve for control variables that satisfy optical or manufacturing behavior. Their shared failure mode is sequential patching. If each local condition is handled alone, a later fix breaks an earlier one. The common mathematical move is to gather the unknowns into one coupled system and solve for all of them at once, often with approximations that preserve the important balances. These papers are siblings because they treat graphics as a negotiation among many small demands. The final image, shape, or motion is the agreement that satisfies the whole negotiation.
solve.dots: The papers under this roof all deploy the same move: take a mesh problem, a material property problem, a shape-intersection problem, or even a physics simulation, recognize it as a system of equations where every variable talks to every other one, and solve them all together. GMT (Geometric Multigrid Transformer) does this for lattice homogenization — thousands of tiny cells in a material, each with stiffness that depends on its neighbors, solved together to predict strength. SharpNet solves Poisson's equation at prescribed edges, the same differential equation that governs heat diffusion and fluid flow, to inject sharp features into neural surfaces while keeping smooth curves everywhere else. Iskra reverses geometry iterations by differentiating through a solver, treating the solve itself as one giant computation you can backpropagate through. The collision and intersection papers (Floating-Point Robustness, Robust NURBS Intersection, Robust Planar Maps) all face the same problem: find where a curve or surface satisfies a constraint (distance equals zero, curves cross, surfaces meet). Instead of trial-and-error, they formulate it as an equation or constraint system and solve it robustly. Even the holography paper (Single-View Holographic Volumetric 3D Printing) balances wave physics and photochemistry in one enormous optimization — light bends, materials harden, and the phase pattern must satisfy both simultaneously. The Hausdorff distance papers (PQ-Free HD, GPU-accelerated Certified) search for the farthest point between two shapes by solving a maximum-distance problem across all candidate pairs; once you set it up as a system, parallelization finds all the maxima at once. What ties them all together: each paper recognizes that greedy, one-at-a-time decisions fail, and that the only honest answer is to solve the entire system together.
solve.picture: Imagine a spider web in still air. Every silk thread touches its neighbors, and together they settle into one stable shape. You cannot set one thread's position independent of the others — when you do, the whole web fights back and re-settles. The web's true shape is the one state where every thread, every connection, every little bit of tension is at rest. That shape is determined exactly by the physics (the weight of the dew, the pull of the frame, the stretchiness of the silk); there is no guessing. A graphics problem works the same way: thousands of points or cells, each pushing on its neighbors, and you must find the one arrangement where everything is satisfied at once.

time.idea: The core problem in animation and simulation is that you almost never have a closed-form answer — no formula that says "at time t, the water is here and the cloth is folded like this." What you DO have is a rule for change: the water flows this direction, the cloth stretches this way, gravity pulls everything downward. So the central move is to march forward in small increments, applying the rule of change again and again. Each tiny step uses the current rate of change to predict the next instant. Repeat a thousand times and you've built motion without ever solving an impossible equation. This is simulation: the practice of taking the largest steps you can without the march spiralling into gibberish.
time.why: The guarantee rests on a piece of mathematical intuition: over a short enough interval, almost everything behaves nearly linearly. If you know how fast something is moving right now, that rate is a trustworthy guide to where it will be one moment from now. When you chain these small steps together, tiny errors don't cascade into chaos—they stay contained. This works because each step is calibrated to the instantaneous rate of change. The art is choosing your step size: too large and errors compound into instability; too small and you waste computation. The method breaks when the underlying change is suddenly very fast (a collision, a phase transition) or when the rate of change itself changes abruptly—which is why real simulation often uses adaptive steps that shrink when trouble arrives.
time.math: The mathematical principle is evolution by small steps. Motion is hard because the final state depends on every state before it. Instead of jumping directly to the end, simulation starts with the present state and a rule for change. The rule may come from forces, velocities, diffusion, collision response, fluid transport, or a learned denoising process. A time step says: use the current change rule to estimate the next state. Repeat this enough times and a full motion, flow, or generation path appears. The key mathematical object is the state: all the positions, velocities, densities, probabilities, or latent values at one instant. The update rule maps one state to the next. Small steps work because over a short interval, a smooth change is close to linear; the current rate is a decent guide for the immediate future. The danger is accumulation. A tiny error repeated thousands of times can become an explosion, a drift, or a fake motion. Good methods choose stable step sizes, implicit updates, corrections, or adaptive rules so each small step respects the physical or learned process it is supposed to follow.
time.family: The time family contains papers whose main problem is change. Fluid papers move mass and momentum forward. Cloth, soft body, and material papers update positions and stresses under forces. Motion papers step bodies, hands, or objects through believable sequences. Diffusion and generative papers reverse a process over many stages, turning noise into structure by repeated refinement. Their shared failure mode is trying to solve the whole future in one jump. A direct jump ignores intermediate collisions, instabilities, and feedback. The common mathematical move is to make change local in time: define what should happen next, then apply that rule repeatedly while controlling error. These papers are siblings because they all understand that motion is not just a final pose. It is a chain of causes, and each link must be plausible for the whole sequence to make sense.
time.dots: Across these papers the same core move appears disguised in many forms. In fluid simulation (Boltzmann, LBM-MPM coupling, two-phase flows), the idea is to track aggregate statistics—momentum and energy densities—and march them forward moment by moment using evolution equations; sand and water couple because each evolves in lockstep while exchanging forces at each step. In elasticity and deformation (Material Point Methods, volumetric elastodynamics), you advance position and deformation tensors forward while solving forces implicitly to stay stable across large steps. In generative models (diffusion-based shape generation, motion synthesis, material transfer), the time-stepping is reversed: you start with noise and refine it step by step, learning at each stage which shapes or poses or materials fit the data better—the diffusion process IS a time-reversal of adding noise, so stepping backward through a learned process recovers structure. In hybrid approaches like motion capture refinement (MOCHI), two methods step forward in tandem: first optimize hand grasp validity, then evolve the full motion using priors. The thread connecting them all is the same: break an impossible global problem into a sequence of small local steps, apply a learned or physical rule at each step, and trust that repetition builds the full answer.
time.picture: Imagine developing a photograph in old-fashioned chemistry: the image doesn't appear all at once, but gradually emerges from a blank sheet as the developer liquid works over time. At each moment the photographer can see what's clearer and what still needs work, and the chemistry keeps pushing forward. This is exactly what a time-stepper does—it starts with an initial guess (maybe noise, maybe a rough pose) and repeatedly applies a rule that says "move toward the target" or "obey physics." With each step the answer gets sharper. Stop too early and it's a blur; stop at the right moment and you have the final picture.
